headline: Athlete stopped at metro station for wearing shorts, DMTCL official 'embarrassed'
summary: Triathlete Sajjad Hossain Snigdho was allegedly harassed by officials who called his athletic attire 'obscene' before eventually allowing him to travel.
details: Triathlete Sajjad Hossain Snigdho was allegedly stopped from entering a metro rail station on Sunday after a police officer called his shorts 'obscene'.
Sajjad reported that he had been training at Ramna Park and was attempting to travel to Zia Udyan for another session when he was singled out from the crowd.
He alleged that officers laughed at him and harassed him, and that senior officials backed the officers' position when he questioned the rules regarding attire.
Sajjad further claimed that officials took photographs of him and that a staff member told him such clothing 'doesn't go with Bangladesh'.
After being detained at the station for nearly 40 minutes, he was eventually granted permission by senior officials to travel.
Major (retd) Mohammad Zakir Siddique, deputy general manager (security) of DMTCL, stated that the authorities are 'embarrassed' by the incident.
Siddique added that the matter has been noted and will be discussed with the managing director to take necessary action following a written complaint.
caption:
Called 'obscene' for wearing shorts: An athlete was stopped from entering the Dhaka Metro Rail.

Triathlete Sajjad Hossain Snigdho was allegedly stopped from entering a metro rail station on Sunday after a police officer called his shorts 'obscene'.

Sajjad reported that he had been training at Ramna Park and was attempting to travel to Zia Udyan for another session when he was singled out from the crowd.

He alleged that officers laughed at him and harassed him, and that senior officials backed the officers' position when he questioned the rules regarding attire.

Sajjad further claimed that officials took photographs of him and that a staff member told him such clothing 'doesn't go with Bangladesh'.

After being detained at the station for nearly 40 minutes, he was eventually granted permission by senior officials to travel.

Major (retd) Mohammad Zakir Siddique, deputy general manager (security) of DMTCL, stated that the authorities are 'embarrassed' by the incident.

Siddique added that the matter has been noted and will be discussed with the managing director to take necessary action following a written complaint.

headline_marked: Over 1,000 [[detained in drives against teen gangs]] across three districts
headline: Over 1,000 detained in drives against teen gangs across three districts
summary: Police conducted massive crackdowns in Cumilla, Lakshmipur, and other areas to curb juvenile delinquency and gang violence.
details: Police detained 1,029 people during coordinated drives against teen gangs across three districts, including Cumilla and Lakshmipur.
In Cumilla alone, multiple phases of operations involving 18 police stations and the Detective Branch led to the detention of hundreds of suspects.
Law enforcement targeted areas with previous complaints of harassment, nuisance, and crime-prone spots to identify those involved in gang activities.
The crackdown follows growing public concern over violence, extortion, and drug dealing by teenage gangs, with some groups openly marching with weapons.
The surge in surveillance was triggered by the killing of 13-year-old Ishiat Shahriar Oprotim, the son of a Comilla University teacher.
Police stated that the prime accused in that murder case, a 19-year-old, had been attempting to form a juvenile gang and recruit other teenagers.
Detainees are currently being screened to determine their level of involvement in criminal activities, with legal action promised for those found guilty.
caption:
Over 1,000 teenagers and youths detained as police launch a massive crackdown on gang violence across three districts.

Police detained 1,029 people during coordinated drives against teen gangs across three districts, including Cumilla and Lakshmipur.

In Cumilla alone, multiple phases of operations involving 18 police stations and the Detective Branch led to the detention of hundreds of suspects.

Law enforcement targeted areas with previous complaints of harassment, nuisance, and crime-prone spots to identify those involved in gang activities.

The crackdown follows growing public concern over violence, extortion, and drug dealing by teenage gangs, with some groups openly marching with weapons.

The surge in surveillance was triggered by the killing of 13-year-old Ishiat Shahriar Oprotim, the son of a Comilla University teacher.

Police stated that the prime accused in that murder case, a 19-year-old, had been attempting to form a juvenile gang and recruit other teenagers.

Detainees are currently being screened to determine their level of involvement in criminal activities, with legal action promised for those found guilty.
